headline: Eleven Songs After Midnight
standfirst: In October 1971 Nick Drake went into a Chelsea studio late at night with one engineer, one guitar and eleven songs. The record they made sold poorly, reached his label in an odd way, and decades later became one of the most quietly influential albums of its time.

sections.heading: After the orchestras
paragraphs: By the autumn of 1971 Nick Drake had made two albums for Island Records, and neither had found much of an audience. *Five Leaves Left* came out in 1969; *Bryter Layter*, delayed over its artwork, followed in March 1971. Both were produced by Joe Boyd and engineered by John Wood at Sound Techniques in Chelsea, and both surrounded Drake's guitar and voice with other people: string arrangements, members of Fairport Convention, and on *Bryter Layter* John Cale and a rhythm section that pushed the songs towards something warmer and jazzier. The records were admired by the people who heard them. Not many did.

Drake was no help when it came to selling them. The handful of concerts he played were short and awkward, with long pauses to retune between songs, and he did not like to talk to audiences or to journalists. Island wanted interviews, radio sessions and gigs to support *Bryter Layter*; Drake refused. Around the same time Boyd, who had championed him from the start, sold his Witchseason company to Island and moved to Los Angeles to work in film music. The person who had built Drake's records around him was gone.

Drake already seemed to know what he wanted to do next. Boyd later wrote that, as they were finishing *Bryter Layter*, Drake told him he wanted to make the next record on his own. In March 1971 he gave what is usually described as the only interview of his career, to Jerry Gilbert of *Sounds*, and said much the same thing: the idea was to work with nobody but John Wood. He had come to feel that the arrangements on the second album were too busy, that the songs had been dressed in more than they needed.

sections.heading: A hard year, and a pause
paragraphs: The year was not an easy one. Drake was living alone in London and withdrawing from the people around him, and in 1971 his family persuaded him to see a psychiatrist at St Thomas' Hospital, who prescribed antidepressants. According to his biographers he was uneasy about taking them and tried to keep it from his friends. Some time before the sessions he went to Spain to stay at a villa belonging to Island's founder, Chris Blackwell, and came back to London in better shape.

It is tempting to hear everything on *Pink Moon* through what came later, and many writers have. The people who look after Drake's estate have pushed back on that. Cally Callomon, who manages it, has said that Drake could not write or record during his periods of depression, that he was not depressed while making this album, and that he was very proud of it. That is worth holding on to. Whatever else it is, *Pink Moon* is the work of a musician who knew exactly what he was doing.

pullQuote.text: Whatever else it is, Pink Moon is the work of a musician who knew exactly what he was doing.

sections.heading: Two nights in Chelsea
paragraphs: Sound Techniques sat in a converted dairy on Old Church Street. Wood had founded it in 1965 with fellow engineer Geoff Frost, and it had become the home of Boyd's roster of folk-rock artists, Drake among them, as well as the place where early records by Pink Floyd and Jethro Tull were made. All three of Drake's albums were recorded there. In October 1971 Drake got in touch with Wood, who had engineered both of his earlier albums, and asked to make another record.

The studio was booked during the day, so the two of them started around eleven at night. Most accounts date the sessions to 30 and 31 October 1971. There was nobody else in the room: no producer, no arranger, no session players. They recorded roughly half the songs on the first night and the rest on the second. Drake sang and played at the same time, as he always had. Boyd once marvelled at how clearly and evenly he picked every note; here there was nothing else in the mix to hide behind, and nothing needed to.

Wood was clear afterwards that the starkness was Drake's choice, not a necessity. "He was very determined to make this very stark, bare record," he said in a 1979 radio interview, adding that he thought the album was closer to who Drake really was than either of the first two. The only addition to voice and guitar anywhere on the album is a short piano part on the title track, played by Drake himself and laid over the top afterwards.

That track, [[Pink Moon]], opens the record. It runs a little over two minutes: a strummed guitar in an open tuning, a quiet voice, and the song's warning that a pink moon is on its way and will reach everyone in the end. Partway through, the piano figure arrives, bright and brief, and it is the nearest the album comes to decoration. The master tape box also listed a short guitar version of the old French song "Plaisir d'amour", but it was marked as a spare not to be used, and it stayed off the record.

pullQuote.text: There was nobody else in the room: no producer, no arranger, no session players.

sections.heading: Eleven songs, twenty-eight minutes
paragraphs: The songs are short, and the whole album lasts only about twenty-eight minutes. Several of them would barely count as sketches on another artist's record, yet none of them feels unfinished. Wood, asked about the length years later, called it "just about right. You really wouldn't want it to be any longer."

[[Place to Be]] follows the title track and sets the tone for much of what comes after: a man looking back at the brightness he had when he was younger and measuring how far away it now seems. [[Road]] is quicker on its feet, its fingerpicking as fine as anything Drake put on tape, while [[Which Will]] turns a love song into a string of gentle questions about who someone will choose and where she will go. The first side's instrumental, [[Horn]], is less than a minute and a half long: a slow guitar melody, one note at a time, that hangs in the air and then stops.

[[Things Behind the Sun]] closes the first side and is the longest song on the album, at just under four minutes. It is a song of counsel, urging someone to see past the crowd and its opinions and to look harder at what lies beyond the obvious, Side two opens with its opposite. [[Know]] is built from a few notes repeated over and over on two strings and a handful of words that seem to contradict each other, and it is as bare as anything Drake recorded.

Wood said that it was [[Parasite]] that told him this record was something different. It is slow and unflattering, a song in which the singer casts himself as someone hanging on at the edges of other people's lives, with a passing image of riding the London Underground. [[Free Ride]] is more agitated, driven by a hard, insistent guitar figure, and [[Harvest Breed]], at around a minute and a half, is a brief and dizzying song about falling. Then the record ends somewhere unexpected. [[From the Morning]] is open and unhurried, full of daylight and renewal, as if the album had been travelling through the night towards it.

pullQuote.text: Several of them would barely count as sketches on another artist's record, yet none of them feels unfinished.

sections.heading: Left at reception?
paragraphs: How the tapes reached Island has become one of the best-known stories in Drake's life, and one of the least settled. In the popular version he walked into the label's offices, left the master tapes at the front desk without a word, and walked out again. Trevor Dann's biography says that he gave them to Chris Blackwell. The most detailed first-hand account comes from Island's press officer, David Sandison, in a 1996 interview for a Drake fanzine.

Sandison remembered coming back from lunch to find Drake sitting quietly in reception with a large master tape box under his arm. He invited him up for a cup of tea, and Drake sat in his office for half an hour or so, said very little, and left. An hour later the receptionist rang up to say Drake had left his tapes behind. Sandison went down, saw the name *Pink Moon* on the box, and realised it was an album nobody at the label knew existed. So the legend is not quite right, but it is not entirely wrong either, and accounts from the people involved don't fully agree.

Island, which had not been expecting a third album, made the most of the surprise. A *Melody Maker* advertisement that February admitted that "the first we heard of it was when it was finished." The label released *Pink Moon* in Britain on 25 February 1972 and spent its whole promotional budget on full-page advertisements in the major music papers that month. Blackwell believed the record could reach a wider audience. His staff were less sure. A&R manager Muff Winwood later recalled his frustration at an artist who would not play live or talk to the press, and said that only Blackwell's enthusiasm kept Drake on the label.

pullQuote.text: So the legend is not quite right, but it is not entirely wrong either

sections.heading: A pink moon to go on
paragraphs: The cover was its own small puzzle. Keith Morris, who had photographed Drake for *Five Leaves Left*, was commissioned to shoot him again, but the pictures showed a hunched, withdrawn young man and were judged wrong for a sleeve. Island's creative director, Annie Sullivan, remembered sitting with Drake as he barely spoke, yet somehow coming away knowing what he wanted. "I had 'pink moon' to go on," she said.

What Island used in the end was a painting by Michael Trevithick, a friend of Drake's sister, the actor Gabrielle Drake. It is a crowded, surreal, Dalí-esque picture, and a sharp break from the photographs of Drake that had fronted the first two albums. Morris's photographs appeared on the inner sleeve. Sandison later found the framed original painting among the clutter of a basement room Island gave him as an office, hung it in his own home for several years, and eventually gave it to Drake's parents.

The reviews were brief and divided. Jerry Gilbert, who had championed Drake in *Sounds*, was disappointed and felt the songs needed more around them, though he picked out [[Things Behind the Sun]] and [[Parasite]] as standing up on their own. Mark Plummer in *Melody Maker* found the music more compelling the longer he listened but felt that it kept retreating from him. In *Time Out*, Al Clark praised the songs and the voice and predicted, sadly and accurately, that Drake would remain a private pleasure for the few who found him. *Pink Moon* sold fewer copies than either of the albums before it.

sections.heading: Far Leys
paragraphs: In the months after the release Drake withdrew further, from performing, from recording and from most of his friends. He went back to live at Far Leys, his parents' house in the village of Tanworth-in-Arden in Warwickshire, and he lived on a small weekly retainer from Island. His sister later described a household whose days rose and fell with how he was. Friends recalled long silences and sudden disappearances. He remained unwell.

He did not stop writing altogether. In February 1973 he called Wood to say he was ready to start on a fourth album, and further sessions followed in 1974, with Boyd back in the room for some of them. His mother remembered how glad the family were to see him happy in the studio again. Four of the songs from those sessions were later released.

Nick Drake died at Far Leys in the early hours of 25 November 1974. He was twenty-six. He had taken an overdose of amitriptyline, an antidepressant he had been prescribed. At the inquest the following month the coroner recorded that he had died while suffering from a depressive illness, and returned a verdict of suicide. His ashes were buried beneath an oak tree in the churchyard of St Mary Magdalene in Tanworth-in-Arden, and the family gravestone carries words taken from [[From the Morning]], the song that closes his last album.

pullQuote.text: He did not stop writing altogether.

sections.heading: Everywhere, eventually
paragraphs: For several years very little happened. Then in 1979 Island released *Fruit Tree*, a box set gathering the three albums with the songs from the late sessions and a long biographical essay by the American journalist Arthur Lubow. It did not sell in great numbers, but it kept the records in print and in circulation. Through the 1980s musicians including Kate Bush, Paul Weller, Peter Buck of R.E.M. and Robert Smith of the Cure spoke about Drake's influence. The first English-language biography, by Patrick Humphries, appeared in 1997, and two documentaries followed in 1999 and 2000.

The moment most people point to came from an unlikely place. In November 1999 Volkswagen unveiled a commercial for its Cabrio convertible called "Milky Way", made by the Boston agency Arnold and directed by Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris. The agency had first planned to use a different song, which is where the title came from, before settling on [[Pink Moon]]. The minute-long film follows four friends driving through the countryside down moonlit country roads at night; when they reach a party, they decide to skip it and keep driving instead. It is barely an advert at all, and the song does most of the talking.

The effect was immediate. In the United States, *Pink Moon* went from selling around 6,000 copies a year to 74,000 in 2000. Boyd remembered Drake, in his last years, asking bitterly why he was not better known. Now a new generation found the record almost overnight, and the early internet, file-sharing included, carried it further still.

Since then the album's place has only grown. Pitchfork gave it a perfect ten in 2014, and *Rolling Stone* placed it at number 201 on its 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. Musicians from José González to Iron & Wine and Bon Iver have been counted among Drake's heirs, and the album stands behind a whole tradition of hushed, close-miked records built on the idea that one voice and one guitar can be enough.

None of that changes the record itself, which still sounds like what it was: two nights, one engineer, eleven songs and a short piano line. It is very quiet and very brief, and it asks nothing of the listener except attention. Played in a dark room, it still feels less like a performance than like being let in on something, briefly, before the door closes again with [[From the Morning]].

pullQuote.text: It is very quiet and very brief, and it asks nothing of the listener except attention.
